title: Omaha Morning Brief
summary: Brent near $110, chip stocks' longest losing streak since 2008, Warsh gives no signal on a hike, and Travelers' quarter before Isaias.

sections.heading: The short version
paragraphs: Good morning, Warren. It is Monday, October 19th. Three things matter this morning. Oil closed Friday at its highest level since May. Chip and artificial intelligence stocks had their worst week in months. And the chair of the Federal Reserve gave no signal on another rate increase, so markets now see one next week as unlikely.

sections.heading: Rates and inflation
paragraphs: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh spoke Friday at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok. He called the artificial intelligence spending boom a shock that raises demand now, before it raises supply, and said the road to higher productivity will be very bumpy. He would not say what the Federal Reserve will do on October 28. Futures now put the odds of a rate increase at roughly one in six.

The 10-year Treasury yield ended the week at 5.09%, down from 5.24% a week earlier. Three-month Treasury bills pay 4.26%. Industrial production rose 0.7% in September, the biggest gain since April. In Europe, inflation rose to 3.8% in September, a three-year high, driven by energy.

sections.heading: Markets
paragraphs: On Friday the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659, and the Nasdaq fell 2.1%. The Dow slipped 0.3% but still gained 0.7% for the week. The S&P lost about 2% for the week and the Nasdaq 4.5%, both their worst week since June.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell for an eighth straight day, its longest losing streak since 2008. It is now about 24% below its June record.
On valuation, FactSet puts the S&P 500 at 19 times expected earnings, measured before Friday's drop. That is an earnings yield of about 5.3%, close to the 10-year Treasury yield.

sections.heading: Companies
paragraphs: In artificial intelligence, the debt worries continued. CoreWeave, which carries about $50 billion of debt, fell about 12% on Friday and about 25% for the week. One of its bonds briefly yielded more than 16%.

Travelers earned $9.18 a share on a core basis. Its combined ratio was 86.8%, which means it kept about 13 cents of every premium dollar as underwriting profit. Net investment income was a record $908 million after tax, and it bought back $1.5 billion of stock. These results come before Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall October 9. Modelers put Isaias insured losses at $1 billion to $4.5 billion.
Truist took a $1.4 billion loss to sell $8.6 billion of old, low-yielding bonds and buy higher-yielding ones. Adjusted earnings rose 12%.
J.B. Hunt's revenue rose 20%, but its profit rose only about 1%. Driver pay, fuel and claims costs took the difference, and management says its prices must catch up in next year's contract season.
In deals, Proofpoint, owned by Thoma Bravo, agreed to buy the data security company Varonis for about $6.3 billion in cash.

sections.heading: The world
paragraphs: Brent crude settled at $109.86 on Friday, up 3.7%, its highest close since May. West Texas Intermediate closed at $101.41. Since Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards have said two supertankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Neither ship has been named, and the claims are not independently confirmed. A British maritime monitor reports the most attacks on shipping in a single week since the war began in February.

Iran's foreign minister says the strait could reopen within days if the United States accepts a seven-day plan sent through Qatar. It requires an end to the naval blockade and to oil sanctions. Washington wants Iran's nuclear program dealt with first. On Friday the Energy Department offered to lend up to 17 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
A correction: on Friday we said China's pause on rare earth export controls ends November 10. The United States says the truce was extended in September to January 10.
China reports third-quarter growth at 10 o'clock this morning, Hong Kong time. Economists polled by Reuters expect 4.4%, below Beijing's target of 4.5% to 5%.

sections.heading: Coming up
paragraphs: Tuesday brings housing starts, General Motors and Netflix. Wednesday, Tesla, Meta and IBM report after the close. Procter & Gamble reports Thursday. Friday brings American Express and the final University of Michigan consumer survey. The Federal Reserve decides on October 28, and the European Central Bank on October 29. That is the briefing. Have a good day.
